introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou` (deux sous-questions « a » dans un même exercice seraient refusées).

Question 5(a)(ii) : le sujet laisse le choix entre deux questions (EITHER industries « foot loose » / OR couloirs maritimes), chacune de 7 marks, à l'intérieur de la sous-question « a » (16 points : (i) 9 + (ii) 7). La règle `ou` s'applique à tout un groupe de sections et ne peut donc pas l'exprimer sans fausser les questions 4 et 6 ; le corrigé traite les deux versions de (ii), signalées « EITHER » et « OR (alternative question) ».

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 6+4+4+6+5 ; Q2 8+8+9 ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 9+9+7 ; Q5 9+7+9 ; Q6 4+6+6+9 ; Q7 EITHER 15+10, OR 5+5+9+6). Les sous-questions regroupant des parties (i) et (ii) (1a, 1b, 5a, 6a, OR-a, OR-b) portent la somme de leurs marks (10, 10, 16, 10, 10, 15) ; les marks de chaque partie restent imprimés dans l'énoncé. Aucun écart avec le sujet.

Défauts d'impression du sujet, transcrits avec le minimum de retouches : Q1(a) « heavy or less precipitation » (formulation maladroite, recopiée) ; Q2(a) se termine par deux points (« surface.. »), un seul conservé ; Q4 « The unven distribution » (faute d'impression pour « uneven », corrigée dans la transcription) ; Q4(c) se termine par une virgule (« sparsely populated, ») ; Q5(a)(ii) une apostrophe parasite devant « Discuss » (non recopiée) ; Q5(a)(ii) OR et Q5(b) se terminent par un point d'interrogation alors que la phrase est une consigne (« Explain... ? », « Explain THREE efforts... sector? »), recopié tel quel ; Q7 la version OR n'est pas numérotée (« OR » puis a), b)) et les parties (i) et (ii) du b) de la version OR sont numérotées « i) » et « ii) » sous « b) ». La page 3 du scan montre en marge gauche des fragments de caractères sans lien avec le sujet, ignorés.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions), filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2026, THREE HOURS, référence GCE26/0750/2/P52. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les trois figures déclarées (profil de sol, courbes de Malthus et de Boserup, rente économique de Von Thünen) sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle, sans valeur numérique.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about », « roughly » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Question 1(c) : la description de la pluviométrie de la zone équatoriale du Cameroun (type guinéen à quatre saisons de 1500 à 2000 mm environ, type camerounais côtier de plus de 3000 mm, Debundscha à plus de 9000 mm certaines années) reprend les chiffres courants des manuels, donnés comme ordres de grandeur ; limites de la zone « au sud de 6 degrés nord environ » approximatives. Question 2(b) : l'exemple de Keta (Ghana) et l'érosion de la côte camerounaise sont cités sans détail. Question 2(a) : dates de Wegener (1912, 1915) et de Pangée (« il y a environ 200 millions d'années ») sont des repères courants.

Question 4(c) : les bassins de Ndian et de Mamfe sont décrits d'après les manuels camerounais (forêt dense, marécages et inondations, maladies, isolement, parc national de Korup) ; aucun chiffre de densité n'est donné. Le point sur l'insécurité récente (régions du Sud-Ouest et du Nord-Ouest) est un fait contemporain cité avec prudence.

Question 5(b) : les actions de l'État cité (barrage de Lom Pangar, Memve'ele, centrale à gaz de Kribi, projet de Nachtigal, port en eau profonde de Kribi, régime des zones franches depuis le début des années 1990, Charte des investissements de 2002, Cameroon Business Forum, stratégies DSCE et SND 2020-2030) sont des faits reconnus mais l'état d'avancement actuel de chaque projet (en particulier Nachtigal) et les dates exactes sont à vérifier. Question 6(c) : taux d'urbanisation « d'environ 55 à 60 pour cent » = estimation récente, ordre de grandeur.

Question 7(a) : exemples cités (crues de printemps de la Red River en 1997, tsunami de décembre 2004 avec plus de 200 000 morts, tsunami du Tohoku en 2011, crues du Yangtsé en 1998 en partie attribuées à la déforestation, inondations de Douala et de Yaoundé) reconnus mais à faire relire ; le rôle de la déforestation dans les crues du Yangtsé reste discuté.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Explain TWO processes involved in the development of soil profiles.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **soil profile** is the vertical section through the soil, from the surface down to the parent rock, made of layers called **horizons** (O, A, B, C and the bedrock R). The profile develops as the parent rock is weathered and the materials are added, removed, moved and transformed. Two major processes are explained below (any two are accepted: the others are listed at the end).

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2026-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

**1. Leaching (eluviation) and illuviation (translocation)**

- **Leaching** is the removal of soluble minerals (calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium salts) by water that percolates downward through the soil. **Eluviation** is the washing out of fine particles (clay) and of iron and aluminium compounds from an upper horizon (the A horizon, the *eluvial* horizon).
- The materials are carried down and deposited in the horizon below, usually the B horizon, by **illuviation** (the *illuvial* horizon). The B horizon is therefore richer in clay, iron or humus, and is often denser and darker or redder than the A horizon.
- The process is most active where **rainfall exceeds evaporation**: it produces a leached, paler topsoil and an accumulation layer below, and it is strongest in the humid tropics (the nutrient-poor ferrallitic soils of the forests of southern Cameroon) and in the cool humid forests (podzols). It is one of the reasons why the horizons differ in colour, texture and chemistry.

**2. Humification (decomposition of organic matter, with mixing by organisms)**

- Leaves, roots and dead animals fall on the surface (the **O horizon**, litter). Bacteria, fungi and soil animals (earthworms, termites, insects) **decompose** them into **humus**, a dark, stable material, and release nutrients.
- Soil organisms mix the humus into the mineral soil (**bioturbation**): this forms the dark, fertile, crumbly **A horizon**, rich in organic matter, which improves the structure, the water-holding capacity and the fertility of the soil.
- The rate depends on climate: decomposition is **fast in the hot humid forest** (little humus accumulates because nutrients are rapidly recycled and absorbed), **slow in cold or waterlogged areas** (peat and thick acid humus).

**Other acceptable processes:** **weathering** of the parent rock (physical and chemical, which makes the regolith, the C horizon), **laterisation** in the humid tropics (loss of silica and concentration of iron and aluminium oxides, giving red lateritic soils), **calcification** (upward movement of calcium by capillary rise in dry climates), **gleying** (waterlogged conditions, grey and mottled soil) and **podzolisation** (leaching under acid conditions).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Examine THREE ways man can disrupt the equilibrium of an ecosystem.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An ecosystem is in **equilibrium** (dynamic balance) when the flows of energy and the cycling of nutrients, and the numbers of the species, remain relatively stable over time. Human activities can upset this balance in many ways. Three are examined (3 marks each).

1. **Deforestation and land clearance.** Cutting the forest for timber, farmland, plantations, fuel wood or roads removes the producers, so the **food webs collapse** and the **habitats** of animals are destroyed and species disappear. Without the canopy and roots, the soil is exposed to rain, **erosion** increases and **nutrients** are washed out of the system (in the tropical forest most nutrients are in the vegetation, not in the soil). The local **climate** and the water cycle also change (less evapotranspiration, less rainfall, more run-off). Examples: the logging and clearing of the Congo Basin forests, including the forests of southern and eastern Cameroon, and the clearing of forest for oil palm plantations in the South-West and the South.
2. **Pollution.** Pesticides and chemical fertilisers, industrial wastes, oil spills and domestic sewage poison organisms or change the chemistry of water and soil. Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers cause **eutrophication** of lakes and rivers (algal blooms use up the oxygen and fish die). Persistent pesticides are passed up the food chain and **accumulate** in the top predators (bioaccumulation), which reduces their numbers. Example: oil pollution in the Niger Delta, and agricultural runoff into lakes.
3. **Over-exploitation of species (hunting, fishing, harvesting) and introduction of alien species.** **Over-hunting and poaching** (bushmeat, ivory) and **overfishing** remove key species, so the numbers of their prey, predators and competitors change and the food web is disturbed (poaching of elephants and primates in the Central African forests). The introduction of **exotic species**, deliberately or by accident, can disrupt the native ecosystem: the water hyacinth covering African lakes and rivers and the Nile perch in Lake Victoria (which caused the extinction of many native fish).
4. (Other acceptable ways) **Overgrazing and over-cultivation** (soil degradation, desertification in the Sahel and around Lake Chad), **bush fires**, drainage of wetlands, mining, dams that change the flow of rivers, and urban growth, as well as human-induced climate change.

**Conclusion.** Each of these disturbances breaks one or more links (producers, consumers, decomposers, nutrient cycle), and if the pressure is greater than the ecosystem's ability to recover, the equilibrium is not restored.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) What should be done to mitigate the negative influence of man on the forest ecosystems in Cameroon?

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cameroon has large areas of dense equatorial forest (in the South, East, Centre and South-West), which are threatened by logging (legal and illegal), clearance for shifting cultivation and plantations, fuel wood and charcoal, bushmeat hunting, mining and road building. The following measures are needed (4 or 5 well explained points).

1. **Sustainable forest management and law enforcement.** Apply the **Forestry Law of 1994** (and its management plans): selective logging with rotation cycles long enough for the forest to regrow, felling quotas and diameter limits, forest **certification** (for example FSC) and traceability of timber; control illegal logging by patrols, check points and heavy penalties, and fight corruption in the forest sector.
2. **Protected areas and the protection of wildlife.** Create and manage national parks and reserves and keep them effective (Korup, Campo Ma'an, Dja, Lobeke, Boumba-Bek and Nki), with trained rangers; set up wildlife corridors; apply bans on hunting protected species and strengthen the fight against poaching and the bushmeat trade.
3. **Reforestation and afforestation.** Replant degraded and logged-over land with native species; require logging companies to replant; protect the catchments and mangroves. This restores the habitats, the soil and the carbon stores.
4. **Better farming and alternative livelihoods.** Teach **agroforestry** and **intensive farming** (improved seeds, fertilisers, fallow management) so that farmers do not need to clear new forest; support alternative sources of income (beekeeping, non-timber forest products, ecotourism, fish farming and the rearing of small livestock to replace bushmeat); promote **improved cooking stoves** and alternatives to fuel wood.
5. **Community participation.** Involve local and indigenous peoples (the Baka and the Bagyeli) in management through **community forests** and by sharing the benefits (a share of forest revenue goes to the local communities), so that they become guardians of the forest instead of its enemies.
6. **Education and international cooperation.** Raise the awareness of the population, schools and companies on the importance of forests; use satellite monitoring of forest cover; cooperate with the neighbouring countries of the Congo Basin (COMIFAC) and with international programmes such as **REDD+** that pay for the carbon stored in standing forests; and plan the use of land (zoning of forest, agriculture and industry).

**Conclusion.** The measures combine law, science and the participation of local people, so that the forest is used within its capacity to regenerate.
